`theme:sector-cement` · confidence: single-source · tickers: ULTRACEMCO, AMBUJACEM, SHREECEM, ACC, DALBHARAT, JKCEMENT, RAMCOCEM

**How it makes money:** Regional bulk commodity; EBITDA/tonne x volume; pricing power from regional consolidation.

**Metrics that matter:**
- EBITDA/tonne
- Capacity utilisation
- Realisation/tonne
- Cost/tonne: power & fuel, freight, lead distance
- Volume growth vs industry
- Trade & premium share
- Net debt/EBITDA
- EV per tonne & capex per tonne

**Value chain and where margins sit:** Limestone (captive mines) -> clinker (energy intensive) -> grinding -> dealers/trade (~70%) and non-trade/institutional. Margins sit with low-cost producers that have captive limestone, WHRS/green power and short lead distance; dealers hold thin margins.

**Cycle drivers:** Housing/infra demand, regional supply additions, fuel prices, monsoon seasonality, consolidation (M&A pricing discipline), elections.

**Lead indicators (public India data):**
- Eight core industries – cement (monthly, Office of Economic Adviser)
- Broker dealer channel checks (monthly price per bag)
- Pet coke & imported coal prices
- Central and state capex (CGA)
- Housing launches (ANAROCK/PropEquity)

**What separated winners from losers:** Winners: cost leadership (fuel, freight, green power), regional dominance, disciplined M&A, low leverage. Losers: high-cost single-region players, debt-funded expansion into oversupply, acquisitions paid at peak EV/t.

**Valuation ranges and peaks/troughs:** EV/EBITDA 12–20x through cycle; EV/t $100–200 (consolidation M&A ~$130–170/t in 2022–25). Peaks: 2007, 2017, 2021. Troughs: 2012–14, 2019.

**Current state (Nov 2026):** UltraTech Q2 FY27: EBITDA/t ₹974 (−~20% QoQ, +₹60 YoY), domestic volume +13.8%, utilisation 71% (66%), PAT +21.3%. Ambuja total cost ₹4,410/t (₹4,182 ex-geopolitical fuel impact). Prices +7–10%/bag in late September, October ~5% above Q2 average. CRISIL saw FY27 EBITDA/t at ₹925–950 vs ~₹1,000 FY26.

**Classic traps:**
- Price hikes announced vs realised
- Capacity race after consolidation
- Paying peak EV/t in M&A
- Ignoring fuel-cost lag (inventory)

Fundsmith Equity launched 1 Nov 2010. To 31 Dec 2025: +612.9% cumulative, 13.8% annualised vs MSCI World +467.6% / 12.1% (fund's annual letter). But 2025 returned only +0.8% vs +12.8% for MSCI World - the fifth consecutive calendar year of underperformance (2021-2025) and the weakest year since inception; the since-inception annualised figure fell from 14.8% at end-2024. Process: three rules - buy good companies (high ROCE, high gross margins, cash conversion, low leverage, resilient demand, no banks or heavy cyclicals), don't overpay (free-cash-flow yield vs bonds), do nothing (very low turnover). ~25-30 holdings. Structural edge: low-fee, transparent fund with a long-horizon UK retail base. Smith blamed 2025 on index concentration in a few mega-caps, passive flows and dollar weakness. Mistakes: owning quality at 30-40x earnings left the fund exposed to de-rating (e.g., Novo Nordisk's 2024-25 collapse; earlier PayPal exit; unverified magnitudes). Lesson: even a sound quality process can lag for five years when style or valuation turns; 'don't overpay' is the rule most often broken. Copyable for Indians: the quality checklist maps well to India's consumer/financial compounders, but valuation discipline (FCF yield vs 10-year G-sec) matters most when quality trades at 60-80x.

`person:sanjay-bakshi` | confidence: **unverified** | tags: india, process, quality, behavior

Managing partner of ValueQuest Capital LLP (New Delhi), adviser to the ValueQuest India Moat Fund; long-time adjunct professor at MDI Gurgaon (behavioural finance and business valuation courses; course details not re-verified here); LSE economics; practising value investor in India for 25+ years. His blog (fundooprofessor) and lectures are among the best Indian writing on moats, Munger-style mental models, 'Lollapalooza' effects and the evolution from Graham-style cheapness to quality. Process edge (as he describes it): buy durable-moat businesses when temporary 'bad news' - regulatory scare, one-off loss, sector panic - pushes the price down, and hold; look for 'clean surprises' (businesses whose hidden strengths show up later in numbers); watch for incentive-caused bias in promoters. Track record: ValueQuest's fund returns are not public in this research - treat any number as unverified. Holdings: specific stock attributions circulating online (e.g., chemical or footwear names) could not be verified and are excluded. Mistakes: he has written about selling great businesses too early and owning cheap-but-poor businesses early in his career (characterisation). Copyable: his framework is entirely public - read the lectures, build a moat checklist (pricing power, switching costs, network effects, cost advantage), and use bad-news events as entry points only when the moat is intact.

`insight:flag-receivable-days-context` · verified

RULE: high or rising receivable days are a hypothesis about revenue quality; resolve it by counterparty, trend and industry norm. BENIGN WHEN: the debtor is a sovereign or AAA customer and the delay is budgetary and visible (HAL: debtor days 227 in FY19, CFO -Rs 7,700 cr; dues cleared FY21, CFO +Rs 15,263 cr); the industry norm is long (EPC, defence, B2B pharma exports to regulated markets) and the company is at or better than peers; days are falling as the company gains bargaining power (Polycab ~84-95 days FY15-16 -> 30-48). SUSPECT WHEN: (1) receivables or unbilled revenue grow faster than sales for 2+ years (Ricoh India; Manpasand per commentary); (2) a large share is owed by related parties (Gitanjali: group firms ~33% of receivables) or by unnamed foreign distributors (PC Jeweller UAE exports); (3) credit periods exceed regulatory or industry norms (Gitanjali-linked LoUs ~360 days vs 90-day norm); (4) receivable days jump right after a revenue surge (Vakrangee 157 -> 319 -> 729 -> 1,301 days); (5) receivables disappear via factoring at quarter end (GE), so low days can also mislead. TEST: receivable + unbilled + contract-asset days vs sales growth, related-party note (amounts owed by related parties), ageing schedule (>180 days share), provisions for doubtful debts, customer concentration; compare with the best peer.

- **id:** `thesis:paper-call:BEL:fy27-order-inflow-25000cr-plus`
- **Method:** promise-tracker credibility · **P(ours)** 0.66 · **P(base)** 0.60 · resolve by 2027-05-31
- **Evidence:** Q2 FY27 call (3-Nov-2026): order book ₹68,717 cr (1-Oct-2026); FY27 inflow so far ~₹7,334–8,000 cr. CMD Manoj Jain: guidance 'order inflow of INR25,000 crores minimum, excluding QRSAM and including QRSAM, INR50,000-plus crores'; NGC (next-gen corvettes) cleared, ~₹20,000 cr from two shipyards expected 'staggered… 99% will come in this financial year'; Shatrughat, Samaghat, HAMMER 'confident to get' before March; QRSAM slipped ~7–8 months ('we may get before March'). In May-2026 (Q4 FY26 call) FY27 inflow guide was '>₹55,000 cr' incl. QRSAM 'very soon'. FY26 actual inflow ₹30,045 cr ('met all guidance parameters'). H1 revenue ₹12,824 cr (+26%) vs 15%+ guide.
- **Why our number differs from base:** The ex-QRSAM floor rests mostly on NGC, which is cleared and in contract with shipyards; BEL has met base-order guidance in recent years. The QRSAM history shows timelines slip, so we stay modestly above base.
- **Base-rate reasoning:** Indian defence PSUs meet their 'minimum' order-inflow guidance roughly 60% of the time; big single orders often slip across 31 March.
- **Resolution rule:** YES if BEL's FY27 total order inflow (orders received 1-Apr-2026 to 31-Mar-2027), as stated in its Q4 FY27 results/call or an April-2027 order-book disclosure, is ≥₹25,000 cr (QRSAM included if received).

Screener: P/E 8.97 on TTM EPS ₹85.4, P/B ~1.3, market cap ₹2.09 lakh cr; but earnings are at a cyclical peak: quarterly OP ₹13,932 cr (Jun-26) and ₹12,814 cr (Sep-26) vs ₹7,500–10,000 cr in the prior eight quarters; H1 FY27 EPS ₹64.7 (≈₹130 annualised). - **O_liq:** IBBI public announcement of liquidation dated in the window. A liquidation row with a blank date counts
  if the company's CIRP admission is in the window or its price series stops in the window; otherwise it is
  counted as "undated" and not used.
- **O_cdel (compulsory delisting / exit for cause):** NSE "Compulsory Delisting" or "Delisting – Liquidation" dated
  in the window; **or** company on the BSE suspended list (no dates published) whose screener price series stops in
  the window (last weekly price ≤ T+5y − 90 days; the stop date is the event-date proxy).
- **O_px:** lowest weekly close in the window ≤ 0.2 × the last weekly close ≤ T (screener's adjusted prices).
- **O_fail = O_liq ∨ O_cdel ∨ O_px** (primary). **O_strict = O_liq ∨ O_cdel** (secondary, no price needed).
- Recorded separately, **not a failure:** **O_cirp** = IBBI CIRP admission in the window (lesson L25: Inox Wind and VA
  Tech Wabag were admitted and survived). Reported: how many flagged / unflagged firms were admitted, and how many
  admitted firms failed.
- **R5** = last weekly close ≤ T+5y (within 31 days) ÷ close at T; missing when the series stopped early (then a
  company with O_fail is "not a winner", one without is excluded from the winner denominator and counted).
  **Winner = R5 ≥ 3.** Price return only (dividends not included).

All three are optional or display-only. With no new inputs, every number is unchanged: all 9 example and live files
were regression-tested, and the Markdown is identical except for the version string and the new exit-bet table,
while the JSON keeps every old key with the same value.
- **Cash tax.** `cash_tax_rate`, or `deferred_tax_share` (deferred tax ÷ total tax expense, so cash = book × (1 − share)),
  plus an optional `cash_tax_rate_end` (year N and the terminal value; defaults to the year-1 rate).
  - FCF_t += NOPAT_t × (t_book − t_cash,t) ÷ (1 − t_book), and the terminal value carries the same term at the end rate.
  - EPS stays on book tax. The cash benefit therefore reaches the 5-year multiple only through `payout_of_fcf`.
  - Use it for capex-heavy filers with accelerated or bonus depreciation. Remember that the annual deferral shrinks once
    capex ≈ D&A and stops growing, so fade it unless you can show otherwise.
- **Reinvestment realism.** `incremental_roic_5y`, or `roic_history` `[{fy, nopat, invested_capital}]` (ΔNOPAT ÷ ΔIC
  over the last ≤6 points).
  - The worksheet then solves the **ROIIC the price implies** on the base path and flags any ROIIC used or implied
    that is more than 5 pts from history.
  - For cyclicals, use a full-cycle window and add impairments back: Kirby's 2022→25 window gives 128%, the
    cross-cycle window 11.7%.
- **Exit-multiple bet (always on, L21).** For each scenario it shows the exit P/E used, the DCF-consistent P/E at
  year 5 and the own median P/E (n ≥ 5), plus the EV of the 5-year multiple at each of the three. It is display only:
  the decision card's EV gate still uses the stated exit.
- Example: `tools/decision/calibration_2026-11-23/US-KEX_v13.json`.
